title: Neutral maximal-torus centralizer: product structure and finite normalizer quotient
statement:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All groups are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type over $k$ [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and all subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness and connectedness have the meanings of [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. Let $G$ be smooth and connected. A torus is a group isomorphic to $\mathbf G_m^r$ for some $r\geq0$, where $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$ [def-sc-gm-ga]; a maximal torus is one maximal under inclusion. Let $T\subseteq G$ be a maximal torus. The centralizer functor is
$$C_G(T)(A)=\{g\in G(A):g_{A'}t=tg_{A'}\text{ for all commutative }A\text{-algebras }A'\text{ and }t\in T(A')\}.$$
It is represented by a closed subgroup scheme. Let $C=C_G(T)^\circ$ be its identity component, with the open-subscheme structure [lem-sfb-group-neutral-component-translates]. Then $C$ is smooth and connected, contains $T$, and is solvable: its successive scheme-theoretic commutator subgroups terminate at $1$. There exists a smooth connected unipotent subgroup $U\subseteq C$ for which multiplication is an isomorphism of group schemes
$$U\times_k T\xrightarrow{\sim}C.$$
Here unipotent means that every geometric point in a faithful finite-dimensional matrix representation is a unipotent matrix, that is, satisfies $(u-I)^N=0$ for some $N\geq1$. Every torus subgroup of $C$ is contained in $T$. A rational point is semisimple if its image in every finite-dimensional algebraic representation of $G$ is diagonalizable; every semisimple point of $G(k)$ belonging to $C(k)$ belongs to $T(k)$. Define
$$N=\{g\in G(k):g_A C(A)g_A^{-1}=C(A)\text{ for every commutative }k\text{-algebra }A\}.$$
The set of right cosets $N/C(k)$ is finite. No assertion that $C_G(T)$ is connected is made.

source.place: Proposition 17.28 and its proof, printed p.360 (smooth nilpotent neutral centralizer and identity component of its normalizer); Theorem 16.47 and Corollary 16.48, printed p.341 (direct product and unique maximal torus); the first paragraph of the proof of Theorem 17.33(a), printed p.362 (semisimple elements in this product and finite normalizer quotient).

proof.text: Represent the centralizer before taking its component. Apply [lem-sfb-constant-source-closed-factorization-locus] with source $Y=T$, parameter scheme $S=G$, target $X=G\times_kG$, closed subscheme $W=\Delta_G$, and map $(t,g)\mapsto(tg,gt)$. The diagonal is closed since $G$ is affine and hence separated by [lem-weil-pbc-affine-source-morphism-separated]; the same observation checks separatedness of all schemes in this application. The resulting closed locus $F\subseteq G$ represents exactly the stated centralizer, including its condition after every algebra extension. Commutation with $T$ is preserved under products and inverses, so $F$ is a subgroup scheme. Under the conjugation action of $T$ on $G$, its functor is also $G^T$. Thus [lem-sfb-torus-fixed-scheme-smooth] shows that $F$ is smooth.

source.place: Proposition 1.92, pp.33--34; Corollary 13.10, p.257, via the torus fixed-scheme formulation.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-group-neutral-component-translates], the identity component $C=F^\circ$ is an open and closed connected subgroup scheme. It is smooth by [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-restrict-open-subschemes]. The commutative subgroup $T$ maps into $F$. Its underlying space is connected: its Laurent polynomial coordinate ring is a domain, so its spectrum is irreducible (also for rank zero). Its image therefore lies in the component containing the identity. By [lem-weil-pbc-morphism-factors-through-open-subscheme] its inclusion factors through $C$. The defining centralizer equations show that $T$ is central in $C$, on all algebra-valued points. A torus in $C$ strictly containing $T$ would also be a torus in $G$ strictly containing $T$; hence $T$ remains maximal in $C$.

source.place: Proposition 17.28, p.360, first sentence; Proposition 1.34 and Corollary 1.35, pp.16--17.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-central-maximal-torus-nilpotent] to the smooth connected affine group $C$ and its central maximal torus $T$. It gives nilpotence and precisely the required termination of the scheme-theoretic derived series. Its central series also gives a finite normal series with commutative quotients, since $[C,C_i]\subseteq C_{i+1}$ implies $[C_i,C_i]\subseteq C_{i+1}$. Thus it satisfies both solvability formulations used below. Since the algebraically closed field $k$ is perfect, [lem-sfb-perfect-solvable-unipotent-torus] supplies a smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup $U\subseteq C$ with torus quotient $D=C/U$.

source.place: Proposition 17.23, p.359, used in Proposition 17.28; Theorem 16.33(a)--(c), pp.335--336; compare Theorem 16.47 and Corollary 16.48, p.341.

proof.text: Let $q:C\to D$ be the quotient map. Its scheme-theoretic kernel is $U$ by [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry]. By [lem-sfb-solvable-torus-complements], $q|_T:T\to D$ is an isomorphism. Put $\tau=(q|_T)^{-1}q:C\to T$. Multiplication $m:U\times_kT\to C$ has inverse $c\mapsto(c\tau(c)^{-1},\tau(c))$: the first coordinate factors through the kernel because its image under $q$ is $1$. Substitution verifies both composites on every algebra, so these are inverse scheme morphisms. Finally, centrality of $T$ gives $(ut)(u't')=uu'tt'$ for all algebra-valued points. Hence $m$ is an isomorphism of group schemes with the direct product group law, not only an isomorphism of schemes.

source.place: Theorem 16.33(d), p.336; Theorem 16.47 and Corollary 16.48, p.341; product used in Proposition 17.28, p.360.

proof.text: Let $S\subseteq C$ be any torus and use the product just constructed to obtain a homomorphism $S\to U$. By [lem-sfb-geometric-unipotence-unitriangular-embedding], $U$ embeds as a closed subgroup of some upper unitriangular group. A split torus $S\simeq\mathbf G_m^a$ is $D_k(\mathbf Z^a)$: its Laurent monomials give the group-algebra basis and its comultiplication sends each monomial to its tensor square. Therefore [lem-sfb-diagonalizable-to-unipotent-trivial] says that $S\to U$ is trivial as a group-scheme morphism. In the product $U\times T$ its inclusion consequently factors through $\{1\}\times T$, which proves $S\subseteq T$ scheme-theoretically. In particular every $k$-automorphism of $C$ preserves $T$: apply this containment to its image of $T$ and to the inverse automorphism.

source.place: Theorem 16.47(a), p.341; its proof uses Corollary 14.18(b), p.284. Uniqueness used in Proposition 17.28, p.360.

proof.text: Choose a faithful nonzero finite-dimensional representation $\rho$ of $G$ using [lem-sfb-central-torus-faithful-weight-blocks] with the trivial central torus of rank zero. On restricting to $T\simeq\mathbf G_m^r$, successive application of [lem-sfb-gm-representation-weight-basis] to its $r$ commuting factors yields a simultaneous weight decomposition: each factor preserves the previous weight spaces because the actions commute. Thus $\rho(t)$ is diagonalizable for $t\in T(k)$. Write a semisimple $s\in G(k)\cap C(k)$ uniquely as $ut$. By [lem-sfb-rational-representation-unipotent-point] applied to $U$, its faithful unipotent realization, and $\rho|_U$, the matrix $\rho(u)$ is unipotent. The matrices $\rho(u)$ and $\rho(t)$ commute by centrality of $T$. Their product $\rho(s)$ is diagonalizable by the hypothesis on $s$. Uniqueness in [lem-sfb-multiplicative-jordan-linear-compatibility] identifies its unipotent part both with $\rho(u)$ and with $1$. Faithfulness gives $u=1$, so $s\in T(k)$.

source.place: First paragraph of the proof of Theorem 17.33(a), p.362; Theorem 9.11, pp.168--169; Proposition 14.6, p.282.

proof.text: Represent the normalizer of $C$ without using a smoothness or connectedness theorem for centralizers. For the conjugation map $C\times_kG\to G$, $(c,g)\mapsto gcg^{-1}$, [lem-sfb-constant-source-closed-factorization-locus] gives a closed locus $L\subseteq G$ where it factors through $C$. Intersect $L$ with its inverse image under inversion. This is a closed affine finite-type subgroup scheme $P\subseteq G$: its points are exactly the elements for which both conjugation and inverse conjugation preserve $C$ after all algebra extensions. Thus $P(k)=N$ with exactly the normalizer definition in the statement. Let $M=(P^\circ)_{\mathrm{red}}$. By [lem-sfb-locally-algebraic-group-identity-component], $M$ is smooth, connected and affine of finite type, has the same underlying space as $P^\circ$, and is a subgroup scheme. Also $C\subseteq M$: inner conjugation by $C$ preserves $C$, its connected image lies in $P^\circ$, and its morphism into that open subscheme factors through the reduction since $C$ is reduced (smoothness and [sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced]). On coordinate rings the last assertion says that a nilpotent pulls back to zero in a reduced ring.

source.place: Proposition 1.83, p.31, and Proposition 17.28, p.360; Proposition 1.34 and the reduced identity component construction, pp.16--18.

proof.text: Conjugation gives an action of $M$ on $C$. For each $m\in M(k)$ it preserves $T$, by the uniqueness of the torus proved above. To promote this to a scheme action on $T$, apply [lem-sfb-constant-source-closed-factorization-locus] with source $T$, parameter $M$, target $C$, and closed subgroup $T\subseteq C$, to the conjugation map. Its closed locus $Z\subseteq M$ contains every $k$-point of $M$. Every element of its defining ideal vanishes on $M(k)$; since $M$ is reduced affine of finite type, [lem-wf-affine-nullstellensatz-vanishing] implies that this ideal is zero. Thus $Z=M$ and conjugation restricts to an action $M\times T\to T$. This is an action by group automorphisms, its inverses coming from inversion in $M$. By [lem-sfb-connected-action-torus-rigidity] it is trivial. Therefore the inclusion $M\to G$ factors through $F=C_G(T)$ as subgroup functors. Its connected image contains the identity, so [lem-weil-pbc-morphism-factors-through-open-subscheme] factors it through $C$. Together with the previous inclusion this gives $M=C$ as closed subgroup schemes of $G$.

source.place: Proposition 17.28, p.360, normalizer argument using rigidity, Corollary 12.37, p.241; reduced-parameter version suffices for rational cosets.

proof.text: Finally [lem-sfb-group-neutral-component-translates], applied to the finite-type group scheme $P$, gives finitely many connected components, each with its open subscheme structure a left translate $pP^\circ$ by a point $p\in P(k)$. A field-valued point kills every nilpotent, so $P^\circ(k)=M(k)=C(k)$. Consequently the rational points of each component form exactly one coset $pC(k)$, and there are only finitely many such cosets in $N=P(k)$. These are the cosets denoted $N/C(k)$; if right cosets are written $C(k)p$, inversion gives a bijection between the two coset sets. This proves the required finiteness without asserting that $F=C_G(T)$ is connected.

source.place: Proposition 17.28, p.360, and the finite normalizer quotient in Theorem 17.33(a), p.362; Proposition 1.34 and Corollary 1.35, pp.16--17.

proof_origin.place: Proposition 17.28 and Theorem 17.33(a); the product is constructed using Theorem 16.33(a)--(d), giving the decomposition of Theorem 16.47/Corollary 16.48. Reduced-normalizer detail added to obtain exactly the rational-coset conclusion.

The delivery changes only the item; statement and stmt_deps are unchanged, and there are no new nodes. The 9 steps follow Milne's route and fill in the scheme-level details. Step 1: the centralizer F is the closed factorization locus for (t,g)->(tg,gt) and the diagonal; it is smooth by torus-fixed-scheme-smooth, since the centralizer is the fixed-point functor of conjugation. Steps 2-4: C=F° is smooth and contains T as a central maximal torus. C is nilpotent; I checked that its central series is a normal series with commutative quotients. perfect-solvable-unipotent-torus gives U, and the direct product comes from tau=(q|_T)^-1 q with the inverse checked by hand. Step 5: a torus maps trivially to U via the unitriangular embedding and diagonalizable-to-unipotent-trivial with D_k(Z^a), so T is unique and preserved by automorphisms. Step 6: uses a faithful representation of the ambient G (faithful-weight-blocks at rank 0), U-point unipotence and Jordan uniqueness, so semisimple points of C lie in T. Steps 7-9: P is the scheme normalizer with P(k)=N; M=(P°)_red is smooth and connected; Nullstellensatz promotes k-point preservation of T to a scheme action; rigidity then gives M=C, and the finitely many components of P give finitely many cosets of C(k). Hypotheses, edge cases (T=1, G=T, GL_2 with its diagonal torus, characteristic p, non-reduced P) and acyclicity are checked; the cited same-unit nodes do not depend on the item. Off-unit citations are Mathlib leaves or slopmaster2-closed nodes, so no tool_uses are needed. lean.statement: theorem neutral_torus_centralizer_cartan_structure (k : Type u) [Field k] [IsAlgClosed k] (G T : Grp (Over (Spec (.of k)))) [IsAffine G.X.left] [LocallyOfFiniteType G.X.hom] [QuasiCompact G.X.hom] [Smooth G.X.hom] [ConnectedSpace G.X.left] (iT : T ⟶ G) (hT : ReductiveTorusCentralizer.IsMaximalTorus iT) : ∃ (F : Grp (Over (Spec (.of k)))) (iF : F ⟶ G), IsClosedSubgroupScheme iF.hom.hom ∧ ∃ (_ : LocallyOfFiniteType F.X.hom) (_ : QuasiCompact F.X.hom), (∀ (A : Type u) [CommRing A] [Algebra k A], Set.range (fun f : StandardGroupSchemes.affine k A ⟶ F.X ↦ f ≫ iF.hom.hom) = ReductiveTorusCentralizer.centralizerPoints iT A) ∧ ∃ (C : Grp (Over (Spec (.of k)))) (eC : C ≅ Grp.mk (GrpObj.identityComponent F.X)) (iC : C ⟶ G) (jT : T ⟶ C), eC.hom.hom.hom ≫ GrpObj.identityComponentι F.X ≫ iF.hom.hom = iC.hom.hom ∧ IsClosedSubgroupScheme iC.hom.hom ∧ SolvableGroupStructure.IsAlgebraic C ∧ Smooth C.X.hom ∧ ConnectedSpace C.X.left ∧ IsSolvableGroupScheme C.X ∧ jT ≫ iC = iT ∧ (∃ (U : Grp (Over (Spec (.of k)))) (jU : U ⟶ C) (e : U ⊗ T ≅ C), IsClosedSubgroupScheme jU.hom.hom ∧ SolvableGroupStructure.IsAlgebraic U ∧ Smooth U.X.hom ∧ ConnectedSpace U.X.left ∧ SolvableGroupStructure.IsUnipotent U ∧ e.hom.hom.hom = (fst U.X T.X ≫ jU.hom.hom) * (snd U.X T.X ≫ jT.hom.hom)) ∧ (∀ (S : Grp (Over (Spec (.of k)))) (jS : S ⟶ C), IsClosedSubgroupScheme jS.hom.hom → MultiplicativeType.IsTorus S → ∃ f : S ⟶ T, f ≫ jT = jS) ∧ (∀ s : StandardGroupSchemes.affine k k ⟶ G.X, IsSemisimpleGroupSchemePoint G.X s → s ∈ Set.range (fun c : StandardGroupSchemes.affine k k ⟶ C.X ↦ c ≫ iC.hom.hom) → s ∈ Set.range (fun t : StandardGroupSchemes.affine k k ⟶ T.X ↦ t ≫ iT.hom.hom)) ∧ Finite (RankOneRoots.Weyl iC)
